newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombia coffee export chief slams speculators.
newsitem.headline: Colombia coffee export chief slams speculators.

text.p: The head of Colombia's coffee exporting association, ASOEXPORT, attacked market speculators for forcing bean prices up to "disadvantageous" levels.

In a radio interview Sunday, Gabriel Rosas also condemned Brazilian coffee growers for flaunting Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) export quotas by selling "all it could" when international prices were hovering around $3 per pound.
"It's been the deliberate actions of market speculators that have helped push coffee prices up to exaggerated, and I would say disadvantageous, levels," Rosas told RCN radio.

Short supplies, in the face of a predicted harvest of about 10 million 60-kg bags in the 1996/97 coffee year in Colombia, coupled with fears of a possible frost in Brazil recently forced international prices above the $3 per pound barrier.
Prices have now dropped back sharply, however, with benchmark September arabicas trading at around $1.80 Friday and July spot fetching close to $2.
Rosas reiterated concerns, already voiced by other major players in the Colombian coffee industry, that excessively high prices could cut consumption in the long-term.

"A market is won over many years, but it can be lost in just five minutes...Coffee is not an essential product, it can be substituted," he said. He did not specify what price level would be reasonable.
The ASOEXPORT chief also blasted Brazil for selling what he said was 1.5 million 60-kg bags more than its agreed export quota to take advantage of high market prices.
"Brazil moved to sell impressive quantities, arguing that it had exchange rate problems...It sold everything it could at top prices," Rosas said.

Despite Rosas' implication that Colombia would have done well to follow suit, most growers complained at the time when international prices rose above $3 per pound that they had little or no crop to sell.
